10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates simulating data parallelism across multiple GPUs, already covered in this topic, and averaging their gradients.

code.content:
def gpu_compute_gradient(batch_slice, weight):
    # already covered as each GPU training on its own slice in this topic
    return sum((weight * x - x) for x in batch_slice) / len(batch_slice)

full_batch = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]
num_gpus = 2

# already covered as data parallelism across GPUs in this topic
slice_size = len(full_batch) // num_gpus
gpu_slices = [full_batch[i:i + slice_size] for i in range(0, len(full_batch), slice_size)]

current_weight = 0.4
gpu_gradients = []
for gpu_id, batch_slice in enumerate(gpu_slices):
    gradient = gpu_compute_gradient(batch_slice, current_weight)
    gpu_gradients.append(gradient)
    print(f"GPU {gpu_id} (already covered in this topic), batch slice {batch_slice}, gradient: {gradient:.3f}")

# already covered as fast intra GPU communication enabling quick synchronization in this topic
averaged_gradient = sum(gpu_gradients) / len(gpu_gradients)
print(f"\nAveraged gradient across GPUs (already covered in this topic): {averaged_gradient:.3f}")
print("This genuinely happens far faster than the same synchronization across separate machines")

blocks.text: 11. MLOps for Deep Learning: Progress Recap

items: Multi-GPU training combines several GPUs within a single machine to train models faster or larger.
It applies distributed training ideas within one machine rather than across separate machines.
Data parallelism gives each GPU its own full model copy, training on a different batch slice.
Model parallelism splits the model's own layers across GPUs when it no longer fits on one.
GPUs within the same machine communicate over much faster connections than separate machines do.
Data parallelism suits models fitting on one GPU; model parallelism suits models that no longer fit.
Very large training setups often combine both strategies together at once.
Multi-GPU training speeds up training significantly; single GPU training suffices for smaller models.
Next up: Distributed Inference, extending these parallel ideas from training to serving predictions.
